cards.grammarNote:
Basic sentences follow **Subject + Verb + Object**, just like English:
**我**(I) + **吃**(eat) + **饭**(rice) = **我吃饭**. Verbs never change for person or tense.
cards.englishPhrase: I eat rice, he drinks tea.
cards.phraseRomanized: Wǒ chī fàn, tā hē chá.

table.title: Word order: Subject + Verb + Object
table.note: 我吃饭 = I eat rice. Verbs never change for person or tense.

cards.english: I am a student. (是 links two nouns)
cards.grammarNote:
**是**(shì) links two nouns: A **是** B = 'A is B'.
**我是学生**(I'm a student), **他是医生**(he's a doctor).
Don't put **是** before an adjective — use **很** instead.

table.title: A 是 shì B = A is B (links two nouns)
rows: 我是学生 wǒ shì xuéshēng
他是医生 tā shì yīshēng
我不是老师 wǒ bú shì lǎoshī
table.note: Negate with 不是. Never put 是 before an adjective — use 很.

cards.english: I am happy. (adjective takes 很, not 是)
cards.grammarNote:
Adjectives act like verbs — **don't** add **是** before them. Use **很**(hěn):
**我很高兴**(I'm happy), **我很累**(I'm tired). Here **很** just links; it only means 'very' when stressed.

contrast.prompt: 'I am happy' — 是 or 很?

a.term: 我很高兴 wǒ hěn gāoxìng
a.gloss: ✓ an adjective takes 很, not 是

cards.english: Are you well? (吗 makes a yes/no question)
cards.grammarNote:
Add **吗**(ma) to the end of a statement to make a yes/no question:
**你好** → **你好吗？**(are you well?), **你是学生吗？**(are you a student?). Word order doesn't change.

cloze.prompt: make it a yes/no question (你好 = you are well)

cards.english: What do you want? (question word stays put)
cards.grammarNote:
Question words sit **where the answer goes** — they don't move to the front:
**你想要什么？**(you want what?), **他是谁？**(he is who?). The answer just replaces the question word.
cards.englishPhrase: What do you want to eat?

produce.concept: Question words stay where the answer goes — they don't move to the front
produce.task: ask: you want what? (= what do you want?)
produce.answer: 你想要什么？nǐ xiǎng yào shénme?
produce.gloss: 什么 sits in the object slot; the answer just replaces it. 他是谁？= who is he?

cards.grammarNote:
Count nouns with a **measure word** between the number and the noun:
**一个苹果**(one apple), **两个鸡蛋**(two eggs). **个**(gè) is the general measure word; drinks use **杯**: **一杯茶**(a cup of tea).

table.title: Number + measure word + noun
rows: 一个苹果 yí gè píngguǒ
两个鸡蛋 liǎng gè jīdàn
table.note: 个 gè is the default measure word; some nouns take their own (本 běn for books).

cards.english: I'll have a coffee. (要 to order)
cards.grammarNote:
**要**(yào) = want / would like — the everyday verb for ordering:
**我要一杯咖啡**(I'll have a coffee). **杯**(bēi) is the measure word for cups and glasses.
cards.englishPhrase: I'll have a cup of tea, thanks.
cards.phraseRomanized: Wǒ yào yì bēi chá, xièxie.

produce.concept: 要 yào = 'I'll have' — the everyday verb for ordering
produce.answer: 我要一杯咖啡 wǒ yào yì bēi kāfēi
produce.gloss: 杯 bēi is the measure word for cups and glasses.

cards.grammarNote:
**想**(xiǎng) + verb = want to do something:
**我想吃**(I want to eat), **我想喝茶**(I want to drink tea). Softer than **要**, which is more 'I'll have / I want'.

contrast.prompt: 想 xiǎng vs 要 yào

a.gloss: 想 + verb = want TO DO (a wish, softer)

b.term: 我要一杯咖啡 wǒ yào yì bēi kāfēi

cards.grammarNote:
**好**(hǎo, good) + a verb = pleasant to do:
**好吃**(good to eat = delicious, for food), **好喝**(good to drink — for tea/coffee), **好看**(good-looking).

table.title: 好 hǎo (good) + verb = pleasant to…
rows: 好吃 hǎochī — good to eat
好喝 hǎohē — good to drink
好看 hǎokàn — good to look at
table.note: A productive pattern: 好 + a verb.

cards.english: I am at home. (在 for location)
cards.grammarNote:
**在**(zài) = to be at / located at:
**我在家**(I'm at home), **他在学校**(he's at school). Structure: Subject + **在** + place.

table.title: Location: Subject + 在 zài + place
rows: 他在学校 tā zài xuéxiào
table.note: 在 = to be at / located at. 哪儿 nǎr = where.

cards.english: I eat at the restaurant. (在 + place before the verb)
cards.grammarNote:
To say where an action happens, put **在 + place before the verb**:
**我在餐厅吃饭**(I at-restaurant eat) — not after the verb like English.

contrast.prompt: Where does 在+place go? (I eat at the restaurant)

a.term: 我在餐厅吃饭 wǒ zài cāntīng chī fàn

b.gloss: ✗ not after the verb like English

cards.english: I go to the park. (去 needs no 'to')
cards.grammarNote:
**去**(qù, to go) attaches straight to a place — there's no word for 'to':
**我去公园**(I go park), **我去学校**(I go to school). Put a time word before **去** to say when.
cards.englishPhrase: In the morning I go to the park.

produce.concept: 去 qù (to go) attaches straight to a place — there's no word for 'to'
produce.task: say: I go to the park
produce.answer: 我去公园 wǒ qù gōngyuán
produce.gloss: 我去学校 = I go to school. A time word goes before 去.

cards.english: in the room (在 … 里 wraps the place)
cards.grammarNote:
Position words wrap the noun: **在 + place + 里/上/下**:
**在房间里**(in the room), **在桌子上**(on the table), **在床下**(under the bed).
cards.englishPhrase: The cat is in the room.

table.title: 在 + place + 里/上/下 (position words)
rows: 在房间里 zài fángjiān lǐ
在桌子上 zài zhuōzi shàng
table.note: 里 inside · 上 on top · 下 under — the position word follows the noun.

cards.grammarNote:
State your job with **是**(shì): Subject + **是** + job.
**我是医生**(I'm a doctor), **她是学生**(she's a student). To ask: **你是做什么的？**(what do you do?).

produce.concept: State your job with 是: Subject + 是 + job
produce.answer: 我是医生 wǒ shì yīshēng
produce.gloss: Ask 你是做什么的？nǐ shì zuò shénme de? = what do you do?

cards.grammarNote:
**喜欢**(xǐhuān, to like) can be followed straight by a verb = 'like doing':
**我喜欢阅读**(I like reading), **我喜欢跑步**(I like running). No 'to' or '-ing' change needed.

produce.concept: 喜欢 xǐhuān (to like) + verb = like doing
produce.answer: 我喜欢阅读 wǒ xǐhuān yuèdú
produce.gloss: No 'to' or '-ing' — just 喜欢 + verb. 我喜欢跑步 = I like running.

cards.english: I am working. (在 + verb = happening now)
cards.grammarNote:
Put **在**(zài) before a verb to show it's happening right now:
**我在工作**(I'm working), **他在唱歌**(he's singing). It's the '-ing' of Chinese.

cards.english: I can swim. (会 = a learned skill)
cards.grammarNote:
**会**(huì) = can, for skills you've learned:
**我会游泳**(I can swim), **我会说中文**(I can speak Chinese). Compare **能**(néng) = able / allowed in a situation.
cards.phraseRomanized: Wǒ huì yóuyǒng, nǐ huì ma?

produce.concept: 会 huì = can, for a skill you've learned
produce.answer: 我会游泳 wǒ huì yóuyǒng
produce.gloss: 会 = learned skills. 我会说中文 = I can speak Chinese.

cards.english: I am happy. (很 + adjective, no 是)
cards.grammarNote:
Describe a mood with **很**(hěn) + adjective — **no 是**:
**我很快乐**(I'm happy), **我很累**(I'm tired). **很** links subject to adjective; it only means 'very' when stressed.

cloze.prompt: I'm happy (mood → 很 + adjective, no 是)

cards.english: I feel tired. (觉得 = feel / think that)
cards.grammarNote:
**觉得**(juéde) = to feel / think that — introduces a feeling or opinion:
**我觉得很累**(I feel tired), **我觉得这个很好**(I think this is good). Follow it with an adjective (+很) or a full clause.

produce.concept: 觉得 juéde = to feel / think that — introduces an opinion
produce.answer: 我觉得很累 wǒ juéde hěn lèi
produce.gloss: Follow it with a full comment: 我觉得这个很好 = I think this is good.

cards.english: I'm a little nervous. (有点儿 + adjective)
cards.grammarNote:
**有点儿**(yǒudiǎnr) + adjective = 'a little / somewhat', usually for something undesirable:
**有点儿紧张**(a bit nervous), **有点儿累**(a little tired). It goes before the adjective.

cloze.prompt: I'm a little nervous (有点儿 + adjective, usually negative)

cards.grammarNote:
**太**(tài) … **了**(le) wraps an adjective = 'too / so':
**太累了**(too tired), **太好了**(great! — lit. too good). A strong feeling, often exclaimed.

cloze.prompt: I'm SO tired! ('too …' → 太 … 了)

cards.grammarNote:
**的**(de) links a possessor to a thing, like 's / my:
**我的手**(my hand), **他的眼睛**(his eyes). For close relationships you can drop **的**: **我妈**(my mom).

produce.concept: 的 de links owner to thing (like 's / my)
produce.gloss: 他的眼睛 = his eyes. Close relations can drop 的: 我妈 = my mom.

cards.grammarNote:
To say a body part hurts, name it then add **疼**(téng, to ache):
**我头疼**(my head hurts, lit. 'I head ache'), **我牙疼**(toothache). This topic-then-comment order is very common.

produce.concept: Say what hurts: (I) + body part + 疼 téng (to ache)
produce.gloss: Literally 'I head ache' — topic then comment. 我牙疼 = toothache.

cards.grammarNote:
A two-syllable adjective takes **的** before the noun it describes:
**软的皮肤**(soft skin), **健康的身体**(healthy body). Single-syllable adjectives often skip **的**: **大手**(big hand).

table.title: Longer adjective + 的 de + noun
rows: 软的皮肤 ruǎn de pífū
健康的身体 jiànkāng de shēntǐ
红的苹果 hóng de píngguǒ
table.note: Single-syllable adjectives often skip 的 (好人 = a good person).

cards.english: two hands (只 counts hands, eyes, ears)
cards.grammarNote:
Paired body parts often take the measure word **只**(zhī):
**两只手**(two hands), **两只眼睛**(two eyes), **一只耳朵**(one ear). Use **两**(liǎng), not 二, before a measure word.

cloze.prompt: two hands (只 counts hands, eyes, ears)

cards.grammarNote: Chinese numbers are logical: 11 = ten-one (十一), 12 = ten-two (十二), 20 = two-ten (二十).

cards.english: two people (use 两 or 二?)
cards.grammarNote: Use 两 (liǎng) before measure words when counting things. 二 is for math and larger numbers.
Use 点 (diǎn) for o'clock. Always use 两 for 2:00, not 二点.
块 (kuài) is the spoken unit of currency. 元 (yuán) is the formal/written unit.

packs.name: Question Words — 什么, 谁, 哪里...

cards.grammarNote: Question words stay in the position of the unknown information — they don't move to the front. 你吃什么 has the same word order as 你吃饭 (you eat rice).
多少 (duōshao) asks about quantities. 多少钱 literally means 'how much money.' No measure word is needed between 多少 and 钱.

cards.english: Where do time words go in a sentence?
cards.word: Before the verb — right after the subject (or at the start).
cards.grammarNote: 我今天去 ✓ / 今天我去 ✓ — but never 我去今天 ✗
Days of the week: 星期一 (Mon) through 星期日/天 (Sun). 星期几？= What day?

packs.name: Word Patterns — Spotting How Chinese Works

cards.grammarNote: 化 (huà) turns a noun or adjective into a verb meaning 'to become X' or 'to make X' — like English -ize or -ify.

cards.english: What does adding 化 (huà) to a word do?
cards.word: It creates a verb meaning 'to become X' or 'to make X' — like -ize or -ify in English.
cards.grammarNote: Examples: 自动化 (zìdònghuà) automate, 美化 (měihuà) beautify, 简单化 (jiǎndānhuà) simplify.
者 (zhě) attaches to a verb to mean 'person who does X'. 作 (zuò) = create/write, so 作者 = the one who writes.
记 (jì) = to record or note down. 记者 = the one who records — a reporter.

cards.english: What does 者 (zhě) do when added to a verb?
cards.word: It creates a noun meaning 'person who does X' — like English -er or -ist.
cards.grammarNote: Examples: 学者 (xuézhě) scholar, 读者 (dúzhě) reader, 工作者 (gōngzuòzhě) worker.
性 (xìng) turns an adjective into an abstract noun of quality — like English -ity or -ness. 可能 (kěnéng) = possible → 可能性 = possibility.

cards.english: What does adding 性 (xìng) to a word do?
cards.word: It creates an abstract noun for the quality or nature of something — like -ity or -ness in English.
cards.grammarNote: Examples: 重要性 (zhòngyàoxìng) importance, 安全性 (ānquánxìng) safety, 灵活性 (línghuóxìng) flexibility.
不 is the everyday negation prefix — it directly contradicts the base word. 可能 (possible) → 不可能 (impossible).

cards.english: What is the difference between 不, 非, and 无 as negative prefixes?
cards.word: 不 (bù) = not / un- (everyday); 非 (fēi) = non- (formal, category); 无 (wú) = without / -less (formal/literary)
cards.grammarNote: Examples — 不方便 (inconvenient), 非法 (illegal), 无条件 (unconditional). 不 is by far the most common in speech.
无 (wú) = without; 聊 (liáo) = chat. Literally 'nothing to chat about' — so: boring, pointless, having nothing to do.

cards.english: What does reduplication do to a verb in Chinese? (e.g. 讨论讨论)
cards.word: It makes the action feel casual, brief, or low-pressure — 'do it a little.'
cards.grammarNote: ABAB pattern: 学习学习 (xuéxí xuéxí) = study a bit; 讨论讨论 (tǎolùn tǎolùn) = have a quick discussion. It softens the request.

cards.english: What does 红红的 (hónghóng de) mean, and why repeat 红?
cards.word: Vividly red / reddish — reduplication of adjectives adds a warm, vivid, or softened feeling.
cards.grammarNote: AA reduplication: 慢慢地 (màn màn de) = slowly and leisurely. The repetition makes the quality feel more alive and gentle compared to the plain adjective.

packs.name: 了 — Completed Action & Change of State

cards.grammarNote: 了 after a verb marks completion. Place it directly after the verb to show the action finished.

cards.romanized: Wǒ mǎi le yī běn shū.

cards.english: She drank a glass of water.
cards.romanized: Tā hē le yī bēi shuǐ.

cards.grammarNote: 了 at the end of a sentence signals a new state or change. Something has shifted — it wasn't raining before, but it is now.

cards.english: I understand now. / I get it.
I didn't eat. / I haven't eaten.
cards.grammarNote: Negate completed actions with 没 (méi) or 没有 (méiyǒu) before the verb. Never use 不 with 了 for completed actions. Drop 了 in the negative.

cards.english: The store is closed now. (it just closed)

cards.grammarNote: Add 吗 to the end of any statement to turn it into a yes/no question.
不错 literally means 'not wrong' — used to mean 'pretty good.'
A polite way to decline or say 'no thanks.'
A common greeting in Chinese, like asking 'how are you?'
Add 吗 to the end of any statement to turn it into a yes/no question. Word order stays the same.
没 here is short for 没有. 没关系 = it doesn't matter / no problem.
很 (hěn) is placed before adjectives and usually required — '我好' sounds incomplete; '我很好' sounds natural.
Negate 很 + adjective with 不: 不很好 (not very good). You can also say 不好 (not good).
太...了 = too... (excessive). 太辣了 = too spicy. The 了 completes the expression.

cards.english: What do you think? Is it good?

cards.grammarNote: In negative sentences, 不 replaces 很. Don't say 不很贵.
非常 (fēicháng) = extremely. Stronger than 很.
No 很 in questions — just adjective + 吗.
有点 (yǒudiǎn) = a little / somewhat, used for slightly negative feelings.
是 is used for identity and classification — not for adjectives or location.
Negate 是 with 不是, never with 没有.

cards.romanized: Zhè bú shì wǒ de shū.

cards.grammarNote: 是 is used for identity and classification. It is NOT used with adjectives — use 很 instead.
Adjectives don't use 是 — use 很 directly. 这很好吃 (This is delicious), NOT 这是好吃.

cards.english: What do you do for work?

cards.grammarNote: Negate 是 with 不是. Never use 没是.

packs.name: 有 & 没有 — Have / Don't Have

cards.grammarNote: 有 (yǒu) means both 'to have' and 'there is/are'. Context makes it clear which.

cards.english: to not have / there is no
cards.grammarNote: 没有 negates 有. Never use 不有 — only 没有 is correct.

cards.romanized: Nǐ zài zhèlǐ yǒu péngyou ma?

cards.english: Do you have it or not? (informal)
cards.grammarNote: 有没有 is a common question pattern: verb + 没 + verb = do you or don't you?
有 means 'to have' and 'there is/are'. Use it to ask whether a place has something.

cards.english: Is there a good place to eat nearby?
cards.romanized: Fùjìn yǒu hǎo chī de dìfāng ma?

cards.grammarNote: 有没有 is a spoken question pattern: 'is there or isn't there?'

cards.english: How long have you had this?

cards.grammarNote: 个 is the default measure word used for people and most objects.
Use 两 (liǎng) instead of 二 (èr) with measure words.

packs.name: Resultative Complements — 吃完, 做好

cards.english: finish eating / eat it all up
cards.grammarNote: Resultative complements attach directly to the verb. 完 (wán) = finished/completed. 吃完 = eat to completion. The compound acts as a single verb.

cards.english: He drank up all the soup.
cards.romanized: Tā bǎ tāng hē guāng le.

cards.grammarNote: Negate resultative complements with 没 before the compound. Drop 了. 不 is not used for completed action negation.

cards.english: Can you finish eating it? (potential form)
cards.grammarNote: Insert 得 (de) between verb and result to make the potential form: V得result = can do it. V不result = can't do it.

cards.english: I can't finish it. / It's too much for me.

cards.grammarNote: Pattern: A 比 B + adjective. A is more [adj] than B. Do not add 更 (gèng) — the comparison meaning comes from 比 itself.

cards.english: This dish is spicier than that one.
cards.romanized: Zhè dào cài bǐ nà dào cài là.

cards.english: This restaurant is more expensive than that one.
cards.romanized: Zhè jiā cāntīng bǐ nà jiā guì.

cards.english: The market fish is fresher than the supermarket's.
cards.word: 市场的鱼比超市的新鲜。
cards.romanized: Shìchǎng de yú bǐ chāoshì de xīnxiān.

cards.english: This is not as expensive as that.
cards.grammarNote: Negative comparison: A 没有 B + adjective = A is not as [adj] as B. 没有 replaces 比 for this meaning.

cards.english: This dish is not as spicy as that one.
cards.romanized: Zhè dào cài méiyǒu nà dào cài là.

cards.english: The supermarket vegetables are not as fresh as the market's.
cards.word: 超市的蔬菜没有市场的新鲜。
cards.romanized: Chāoshì de shūcài méiyǒu shìchǎng de xīnxiān.

cards.english: This is a little sweeter than that.
cards.grammarNote: Add 一点 after the adjective to say 'a little more.' Add 多了 or 得多 to say 'much more.'

cards.english: This place is much cheaper than that one.
cards.romanized: Zhè jiā bǐ nà jiā piányí duō le.

cards.english: The flavor here is much better than there.
cards.word: 这里的味道比那里的好得多。
cards.romanized: Zhèlǐ de wèidào bǐ nàlǐ de hǎo de duō.

packs.name: 要 & 想 — Want / Would Like

cards.grammarNote: 要 is more direct. Use it to order food or state a firm intention.
想 is softer, more tentative — like 'I'd like to' or 'I'm thinking of.'

cards.romanized: Wǒ xiǎng yào yī bēi kāfēi.

cards.english: What do you want to eat?

cards.romanized: Wǒ yào mǐfàn, bú yào miàntiáo.

cards.grammarNote: 不要 is a firm refusal.

cards.english: What would you like to drink?

cards.grammarNote: 要 (yào) expresses a firm desire or plan. Stronger than 想 — closer to 'I'm going to' or 'I need to'.
想 (xiǎng) is softer than 要 — a wish or intention without being definite.

cards.english: I want to be a teacher.
What do you want to do?
She wants to be an artist.
I don't want to work overtime.
He needs to find a job.
Where do you want to go?

packs.name: Direction Complements — 上来, 出去, 回来

cards.grammarNote: Direction complements = direction word (进/出/上/下/回/过) + 来 or 去. 来 = toward the speaker. 去 = away from the speaker. 进来 = come in (moving inward toward speaker).
Same direction word, different 来/去 based on whether movement is toward or away from the speaker. Context makes it clear which to use.

cards.english: The food has been brought up / is being served.
She ran out of the hotel.
cards.romanized: Tā cóng jiǔdiàn pǎo chū qù le.

packs.name: Location Word Patterns — 店馆场院站

cards.grammarNote: Chinese location names are built from recognizable suffixes. Learn the suffix and you can guess what a new place is — 咖啡店 (coffee shop), 图书馆 (library), 机场 (airport). These suffixes carry consistent meaning across hundreds of place names.
店 = shop or store. Attaches to a product or service: 咖啡店 (coffee shop), 书店 (bookstore), 药店 (pharmacy), 花店 (flower shop), 面包店 (bakery). If you see 店, it sells something.
咖啡 (coffee) + 店 (shop) = coffee shop. The product always comes first, then 店.
书 (book) + 店 = bookstore. Same pattern: 玩具店 (toy store), 服装店 (clothing store).
馆 = a public hall or cultural/service establishment. 图书馆 (library), 博物馆 (museum), 饭馆 (restaurant), 体育馆 (gym/stadium). 馆 implies a more formal, often public or cultural space than 店.
图书 (books/documents) + 馆 = library. 图书 is a formal word for books — more so than just 书.
博物 (broad knowledge of things) + 馆 = museum. 博 = broad/erudite, 物 = things/objects.
饭 (cooked rice / food) + 馆 = restaurant. 饭馆 is informal; 餐厅 (cāntīng) is more formal. Both are common.
场 = open ground or large functional area. 机场 (airport), 广场 (plaza), 停车场 (parking lot), 操场 (sports field/playground). 场 suggests an outdoor or large-scale space.
机 (machine / plane, short for 飞机) + 场 (field) = airport. 飞机 = airplane; 机场 = airplane field.
广 (broad/wide) + 场 = broad open space = plaza or square.
院 = institution, often formal or official. 医院 (hospital), 电影院 (cinema), 法院 (court), 学院 (college/academy). 院 carries a sense of an enclosed, organized institution.
医 (medicine / healing) + 院 (institution) = hospital. 医生 (doctor) shares the same 医 character.
电影 (movie) + 院 (hall/institution) = cinema. 电影 = electric shadow (a poetic original term for film).
站 = a stopping/transit point. 火车站 (train station), 公交站 (bus stop), 地铁站 (subway station), 加油站 (gas station). If you need to catch transportation, look for 站.
火车 (train, lit: fire vehicle) + 站 (station) = train station. 火 = fire, 车 = vehicle.
地铁 (subway, lit: underground iron) + 站 = subway station. 地 = ground/earth, 铁 = iron/metal.

cards.english: What kind of place is a 大学图书馆?
cards.grammarNote: 大学 (university) + 图书 (books) + 馆 (hall) = university library. Once you know these suffixes, you can decode unfamiliar place names by recognizing the suffix.

cards.english: How do I get from here to the subway station?
cards.word: 从这里到地铁站怎么走？
cards.romanized: Cóng zhèlǐ dào dìtiě zhàn zěnme zǒu?
cards.grammarNote: 从...到... = from...to... for both place and time. The whole phrase comes before the main verb. 从 marks the starting point; 到 marks the destination.

cards.english: How long does it take from Beijing to Shanghai?
cards.word: 从北京到上海要多长时间？
cards.romanized: Cóng Běijīng dào Shànghǎi yào duō cháng shíjiān?

cards.english: It's not far from the hotel to the airport.
cards.romanized: Cóng jiǔdiàn dào jīchǎng bù yuǎn.

cards.english: It takes ten minutes to walk from the park to the library.
cards.word: 从公园到图书馆走路要十分钟。
cards.romanized: Cóng gōngyuán dào túshūguǎn zǒulù yào shí fēnzhōng.

cards.grammarNote: 从...到... also expresses time spans. 从早上到晚上 = from morning to evening.

cards.english: He works from Monday to Saturday.
cards.word: 他从星期一工作到星期六。
cards.romanized: Tā cóng xīngqīyī gōngzuò dào xīngqīliù.

cards.grammarNote: 到 alone as a verb means to arrive. 到了 = arrived (with change-of-state 了). Very common when arriving at a destination.

cards.english: How far is it from home to the office?
cards.romanized: Cóng jiā dào bàngōngshì yǒu duō yuǎn?

cards.english: The shop is open from nine to nine.
cards.romanized: Shāngdiàn cóng jiǔ diǎn kāi dào jiǔ diǎn.

cards.grammarNote: 去 = movement away from the speaker's current position.
来 = movement toward the speaker.
了 marks that the action has begun or just happened.
在 is used to express where someone or something is.
在 + verb = currently doing something (progressive action).
在 before a verb shows the action is happening right now.

cards.english: The store is on the left.

packs.name: Frequency Expressions — 常常, 有时候, 从来不

cards.grammarNote: Frequency adverbs go before the verb in Chinese, usually after the subject. They cannot go after the verb the way some English adverbs can.
从来不 = have never / never do (habitual). 从来没有 = have never done (completed). Both go before the verb.

cards.english: I exercise three times a week.
cards.romanized: Wǒ měi zhōu yùndòng sān cì.
cards.grammarNote: Use 次 (cì) after a number to count how many times. Place the frequency phrase (number + 次) after the verb.

cards.english: Could you take a quick look for me?
cards.romanized: Nǐ néng bāng wǒ kàn yīxià ma?
cards.grammarNote: V + 一下 (yīxià) = do briefly / casually, or softens a request. 一下 makes the action sound lighter and less demanding.

packs.name: Job Title Patterns — 师员家生人

cards.grammarNote: Chinese job titles are built from a small set of suffixes that signal what kind of role a person has. 老师, 工程师, 厨师 all end in 师. Once you recognize these suffixes, you can guess what an unfamiliar job title means.

师 = a skilled, often trained professional. Implies mastery of a craft or discipline. 老师 (teacher), 工程师 (engineer), 厨师 (chef), 律师 (lawyer), 医师 (physician), 设计师 (designer). If the job requires serious skill or training, it often takes 师.
老 (old/respected) + 师 (master) = teacher. 老 here is a respectful prefix, not about age. 老师 is also used as a direct address: 'Hello, teacher' = 老师好.
工程 (engineering/project) + 师 (skilled professional) = engineer. 工 = work, 程 = process/procedure.
厨 (kitchen) + 师 (skilled practitioner) = chef. 厨房 = kitchen (kitchen + room). 厨师 is specifically a professional cook.
律 (law / rule) + 师 = lawyer. 律法 = law/legal code.

cards.english: 员 — staff member / person in a role
cards.grammarNote: 员 = a person who fills a defined functional role, often in a service or organizational context. 服务员 (waiter/service staff), 演员 (actor), 售货员 (sales clerk), 运动员 (athlete), 营业员 (clerk). 员 implies a role within a system, not necessarily a specialized craft.
服务 (service) + 员 (person in role) = service person / waiter. 服务员！ is how you call a waiter in a restaurant — completely normal and not rude.
演 (to perform/act) + 员 = actor/performer. 演 also appears in 演讲 (speech/lecture) and 演出 (performance/show).
运动 (sports / exercise) + 员 = athlete. 运动 also means 'to exercise': 我喜欢运动 = I like sports.

cards.english: 家 — expert / master in a field
cards.grammarNote: 家 = an authority or creative master in a field. Often used for intellectual, artistic, or scholarly domains. 音乐家 (musician), 艺术家 (artist), 科学家 (scientist), 作家 (writer), 画家 (painter). 家 implies depth of expertise, not just a job role.
音乐 (music) + 家 (master/expert) = musician (in the serious, artistic sense). 音 = sound, 乐 = music/joy.
艺术 (art) + 家 = artist. 艺 = skill/art, 术 = technique/method.
作 (to write/make/do) + 家 = writer/author. 作家 specifically refers to literary or creative writers, not journalists (记者) or copywriters.

cards.english: 生 — person in a learning or medical role
cards.grammarNote: 生 = a person who is learning or practicing (especially medicine or study). 学生 (student), 医生 (doctor), 研究生 (graduate student), 实习生 (intern). 生 implies someone developing or applying knowledge — either as a learner or a practitioner.
医 (medicine/healing) + 生 (practitioner) = doctor. 医院 (hospital) shares the same 医. 大夫 (dàifu) is an alternative informal word for doctor.
学 (to learn/study) + 生 (person) = student. 学习 = to study (学 + 习 = learn + practice).

人 = person. Used to form nationalities and broad categories: 中国人 (Chinese person), 美国人 (American), 商人 (businessman), 工人 (worker), 本地人 (local person). 人 is the most general people-suffix — less about skill, more about identity or category.
商 (commerce/trade) + 人 = businessman. 商业 = business/commerce, 商店 = store/shop (商 + 店!).

cards.english: What's the difference: 音乐师, 音乐员, 音乐家?
cards.word: 师 = trained professional, 员 = role-filler, 家 = creative master
cards.grammarNote: 音乐师 = music teacher/instructor (trained skill). 音乐员 = a musician in an ensemble/band (role). 音乐家 = a musician of high artistic standing (master). The suffix shifts the nuance: skill → role → mastery.
会 = a skill you have learned, like speaking a language or driving.
能 = physically able to, or circumstances allow it.
可以 = it is allowed / permissible.
能 is used because circumstances (schedule) prevent it.
可以 = asking for permission.

cards.romanized: Tā huì shuō sān zhǒng yǔyán.
Wǒ bù néng qù, wǒ hěn máng.
Wǒ kěyǐ wèn yí gè wèntí ma?

cards.grammarNote: 不行 (bù xíng) = won't work / can't — a common informal way to say no.
能 (néng) = physically able to, or permitted by circumstances. Used when a condition makes it possible.
可以 (kěyǐ) = permitted to / allowed to. Used to seek or grant permission.

cards.english: Can I walk (am I able to)?

cards.grammarNote: 喜欢 can be followed by a noun or a verb.

cards.english: What do you like to do?

cards.grammarNote: 都 (dōu) = both / all.

cards.english: I like it more and more.
cards.grammarNote: 越来越 = more and more.

cards.english: I like spending time with friends.
cards.romanized: Wǒ xǐhuān hé péngyou zài yīqǐ.

cards.grammarNote: 正在 + verb = currently doing (right now). 正 adds emphasis on the 'right now' aspect. 正在 can also appear as just 在 for a lighter form.

cards.english: I'm working right now. (with 呢 for emphasis)

cards.grammarNote: 在 alone (without 正) is also a valid progressive marker. 在 + verb = currently doing. Slightly less emphatic than 正在.
呢 alone at the end of a sentence can signal an ongoing action, often implying the situation is still going on or asking the listener not to interrupt.
Negation: 没有在 or 没在 before the verb. Never use 不在 for this meaning — 不在 means 'not at a place.'
不 negates verbs and adjectives. Tone changes to bú before a 4th-tone syllable.
Use 没/没有 to negate 有 or to say something did not happen.
Always use 没有 to negate 有.
没 negates a past action — something that didn't happen.
过 marks experience; 没 negates it.
不错 literally 'not wrong' — means pretty good.
没 = didn't (past). 不 = won't / don't (present/future intention).
不 (bù) negates most verbs and adjectives. Changes to bú before 4th-tone syllables.
没 is short for 没有. Use it to negate 有 or to say an action hasn't happened yet.

cards.english: Because I'm very tired, I'm irritable.
cards.word: 因为很累，所以我很烦躁。
cards.romanized: Yīnwèi hěn lèi, suǒyǐ wǒ hěn fánzào.
cards.grammarNote: In Chinese, 因为 and 所以 are usually used together: because...therefore... This differs from English, where you pick one (because OR so, not both).

cards.english: Because he was late, everyone was angry.
cards.word: 因为他迟到了，所以大家都很生气。
cards.romanized: Yīnwèi tā chídào le, suǒyǐ dàjiā dōu hěn shēngqì.

cards.english: Because the weather is nice, I'm happy.
cards.word: 因为天气很好，所以我很开心。
cards.romanized: Yīnwèi tiānqì hěn hǎo, suǒyǐ wǒ hěn kāixīn.

cards.english: Because there's too much work, I'm anxious.
cards.word: 因为工作太多，所以我很焦虑。
cards.romanized: Yīnwèi gōngzuò tài duō, suǒyǐ wǒ hěn jiāolǜ.

cards.english: Because it rained, we cancelled our plans.
cards.word: 因为下雨，我们取消了计划。
cards.romanized: Yīnwèi xià yǔ, wǒmen qǔxiāo le jìhuà.
cards.grammarNote: 因为 can appear alone (without 所以) when giving a reason, especially answering a 为什么 question.

cards.english: Because she was very sad, she cried.
cards.romanized: Yīnwèi tā hěn nánguò, tā kū le.

cards.english: He was late, so I was angry.
cards.word: 他迟到了，所以我很生气。
cards.romanized: Tā chídào le, suǒyǐ wǒ hěn shēngqì.
cards.grammarNote: 所以 can appear alone when the cause is already known or has been stated. It introduces the result/consequence.

cards.english: I didn't sleep well, so I'm very tired today.
cards.word: 我没睡好，所以今天很累。
cards.romanized: Wǒ méi shuì hǎo, suǒyǐ jīntiān hěn lèi.

cards.english: She was very upset, so she cried.
cards.romanized: Tā hěn nánguò, suǒyǐ kū le.

cards.english: Because the news was good, everyone was excited.
cards.word: 因为消息很好，所以大家都很兴奋。
cards.romanized: Yīnwèi xiāoxi hěn hǎo, suǒyǐ dàjiā dōu hěn xīngfèn.

cards.english: Because I haven't heard from him, I'm worried.
cards.word: 因为没有他的消息，所以我很担心。
cards.romanized: Yīnwèi méiyǒu tā de xiāoxi, suǒyǐ wǒ hěn dānxīn.

cards.english: Because it went well, I feel relieved.
cards.word: 因为进行顺利，所以我感到宽慰。
cards.romanized: Yīnwèi jìnxíng shùnlì, suǒyǐ wǒ gǎndào kuānwèi.

cards.word: 虽然很难，但是我很开心。
cards.romanized: Suīrán hěn nán, dànshì wǒ hěn kāixīn.
cards.grammarNote: 虽然...但是... = although...but... Both halves are typically used together in Chinese, unlike English where you choose one. This is a concession pattern.

cards.english: Although tired, I feel very satisfied.
Although he's very busy, he always helps others.
cards.word: 虽然他很忙，但是他总是帮助别人。
cards.romanized: Suīrán tā hěn máng, dànshì tā zǒngshì bāngzhù biérén.

cards.english: Although the weather was bad, we still went out.
cards.word: 虽然天气不好，但是我们还是出去了。
cards.romanized: Suīrán tiānqì bù hǎo, dànshì wǒmen háishi chūqù le.

cards.english: Although I'm very sad, I understand.
cards.word: 虽然很伤心，但是我理解。
cards.romanized: Suīrán hěn shāngxīn, dànshì wǒ lǐjiě.

cards.english: Although the pressure was great, he didn't give up.
cards.word: 虽然压力很大，但是他没有放弃。
cards.romanized: Suīrán yālì hěn dà, dànshì tā méiyǒu fàngqì.

cards.english: I really want to go, but I'm a bit tired.
cards.romanized: Wǒ hěn xiǎng qù, búguò yǒudiǎn lèi.
cards.grammarNote: 不过 (búguò) = however / but — softer and more conversational than 但是. Common in casual speech.

cards.english: She said she was happy, but she looked upset.
cards.word: 她说很开心，可是看起来很难过。
cards.romanized: Tā shuō hěn kāixīn, kěshì kàn qǐlái hěn nánguò.
cards.grammarNote: 可是 (kěshì) = but — slightly softer than 但是. Both 可是 and 不过 are common alternatives in everyday speech.

cards.english: Although I was nervous, I did well.
cards.word: 虽然很紧张，但是我表现得很好。
cards.romanized: Suīrán hěn jǐnzhāng, dànshì wǒ biǎoxiàn de hěn hǎo.

cards.english: Although I was angry, I stayed calm.
cards.word: 虽然很生气，但是我保持了平静。
cards.romanized: Suīrán hěn shēngqì, dànshì wǒ bǎochí le píngjìng.

cards.english: Although I'm stressed, I'm still happy.
cards.word: 虽然有压力，但是我还是很开心。
cards.romanized: Suīrán yǒu yālì, dànshì wǒ háishi hěn kāixīn.

cards.english: Although she cried, she's fine now.
cards.word: 虽然她哭了，但是现在没事了。
cards.romanized: Suīrán tā kū le, dànshì xiànzài méishì le.

cards.grammarNote: Degree complement structure: Verb + 得 + description. 得 (de) links the verb to a phrase describing how the action was done. It's like saying 'to the degree that...'
To ask how well an action was done: V + 得 + 怎么样?
Negation: V + 得 + 不 + description. Insert 不 before the descriptive adjective.

cards.romanized: Nǐ zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo!
Nǐ pǎo de tài kuài le.

cards.grammarNote: In Chinese, body part + 疼 — no 'my' required.
了 indicates the fever has come on.
越来越 + adjective/verb = more and more / increasingly. It expresses a continuing change in one direction.

cards.english: My health is getting better and better.
cards.romanized: Wǒ de shēntǐ yuè lái yuè hǎo le.

cards.english: My legs are hurting more and more.
cards.romanized: Wǒ de tuǐ yuè lái yuè téng.

cards.english: After walking so far, I'm getting more and more tired.
cards.word: 走了这么远，我越来越累。
cards.romanized: Zǒu le zhème yuǎn, wǒ yuè lái yuè lèi.

cards.english: The more I eat, the more I want to eat.
cards.grammarNote: 越...越... links two actions that escalate together. The first 越 sets the condition; the second 越 gives the consequence.

cards.english: The more I walk, the more tired I get.
The more rest you get, the better.
His illness is getting more and more serious.
cards.romanized: Tā de bìng yuè lái yuè zhòng.

cards.english: The doctor is getting more and more worried.
